Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 69:

﴿Say: Indeed, those who invent lies against Allah will not succeed.﴾ [By attributing a son to Him.] ﴿Will not succeed﴾ means they will not be saved from the Fire, nor will they attain success with Paradise. (p-33)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 70:

﴿A brief enjoyment in this world﴾, meaning: their fabrication of this (lie) is a small benefit, which is the world, where they maintain their leadership in disbelief and their hostility toward the Prophet (ﷺ) by displaying it. ﴿Then to Us is their return; then We shall make them taste the severe punishment﴾, the everlasting one, ﴿because they used to disbelieve﴾, that is, because of their disbelief.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 10, verse 71:**

﴿And recite to them﴾ means read to them ﴿the account of Nuh﴾, his story with his people. The pause (waqf) at this point is obligatory, because if it were joined to what follows, ﴿إذ﴾ (idh, "when") would become a temporal adverb (zarf) governed by ﴿واتْلُ﴾ (wat-lu, "recite"). Rather, the implied meaning is: ﴿and mention, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of Allah has been burdensome to you"﴾. ﴿كَبُرَ﴾ (kabura) means it was great and heavy, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed it is burdensome except for the humble﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45].

﴿مَقامِي﴾ (maqami) means my place, referring to himself, as in His saying: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], meaning he feared his Lord. Or it means my standing and my remaining among you for a thousand years less fifty years. Or it means my standing ﴿and my reminding you of the signs of Allah﴾, because when they gave admonition to a group they would stand on their feet and admonish them, so that their place would be clear and their words audible.

﴿فَعَلى اللهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ﴾ means: so I have entrusted my affair to Him.

﴿فَأجْمِعُوا أمْرَكُمْ﴾ (fa-ajmi'u amrakum, "so resolve your plan") comes from ajma'a al-amr, meaning to intend it and determine upon it.

﴿وَشُرَكاءَكُمْ﴾ (wa shuraka'akum, "and your associates"): the wāw here means "with" (ma'a), i.e., so resolve your plan together with your associates.

﴿ثُمَّ لا يَكُنْ أمْرُكم عَلَيْكم غُمَّةً﴾ means: then let your affair not be a distress (ghumma) upon you, and a worry. Al-ghamm and al-ghumma are like al-karb and al-kurba (both meaning distress). Or it means something ambiguous and hidden. Al-ghumma is also a covering, from ghammahu when he covered it. From this comes the hadith: "There is no concealment (ghumma) in the obligations of Allah," meaning there is no concealing them; rather, they must be made public. The meaning is: let your intention to destroy me not remain hidden from you, but be open and publicly known, so that you proclaim it against me.

﴿ثُمَّ اقْضُوا إلَيَّ﴾ means: then carry out to me that matter which you intend against me. That is: fulfill to me what is your due of destroying me, as a man settles his debt with his creditor. Or it means: do whatever you are able to do.

﴿وَلا تُنْظِرُونِ﴾ means: and do not give me respite.

(p-34)

﴿Then if you turn away﴾, i.e., if you turn away from my reminder and my counsel, ﴿then I have not asked you for any wage﴾. Here the turning away is treated as the cause (فَأوْجَبَ التَوَلِّيَ), or the meaning is: "then I have not asked you for any wage, so your turning away has not cost me anything" (فَفاتَنِي ذَلِكَ بِتَوَلِّيكم). ﴿My wage is only from Allah﴾, which is the reward that He will give me in the Hereafter. That is: I have advised you only for the sake of Allah, not for any worldly purpose. In this there is an indication of the prohibition of taking a wage for teaching the Qur'an and religious knowledge. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, among those who submit to His commands and prohibitions. The reading "إنْ أجْرِيَ" with a fatha (on the alif of إنْ, i.e., "inna" with the ya' vowelled as fatha in أجري) is transmitted by Madani, Shami, Abu 'Amr and Hafs.

ﷻ

﴿So they denied him﴾, meaning they persisted in their denial of him. ﴿So We delivered him﴾ from the drowning, ﴿and those with him in the ark﴾, ﴿and We made them successors﴾, who succeed those destroyed by drowning in the ship. ﴿And We drowned those who denied Our signs. So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾. This is a magnification of what befell them, a warning to those whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) warned lest the like of it befall them, and a consolation to him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 74:

﴿Then We sent after him⁠﴾ — after Nuh (peace be upon him) — ﴿messengers to their peoples﴾, that is: Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut and Shu'ayb. ﴿And they came to them with clear proofs﴾, with evident arguments establishing their claim. ﴿But they were not such as to believe﴾, so they persisted in disbelief after the coming (of the messengers), ﴿in what they had denied before﴾, that is, before their coming. He means that before the sending of the messengers they were a people of ignorance (jahiliyyah), denying the truth; so there was no difference between their state after the sending of the messengers and before it, as if no one had been sent to them. ﴿Thus do We seal﴾, with a sealing like that, We set a seal ﴿upon the hearts of the transgressors﴾, those who exceed the limit in denial.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 75:

﴿Then We sent after them﴾ after the messengers, ﴿Musa and Harun to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our signs﴾, that is, with the nine signs. ﴿But they waxed proud﴾ against accepting them. The greatest form of pride is that servants should treat the message of their Lord with contempt after it has become clear, and magnify themselves against accepting it. ﴿And they were a guilty people﴾: disbelievers (p-35) possessing great sins; therefore they grew proud against them and dared to reject them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 76:

﴿When the truth came to them from Us﴾: when they recognised that it was the truth and that it was from Allah, ﴿they said﴾ — because of their love of desires — ﴿"This is clearly magic."﴾ And they knew that the truth is farthest of all things from magic.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 77:

﴿Mūsā said, "Do you say this of the truth when it has come to you?"﴾ It is a rebuke (inkār), and what they said is omitted, i.e., "This is sorcery." Then he began another rebuke, saying, ﴿Is this sorcery?﴾ The "khabar" (predicate) and the "mubtada'" (subject) here: ﴿and the sorcerers do not prosper﴾, i.e., they do not triumph.

"They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon?"" (that is, from the worship of idols, or the worship of Pharaoh), "and that greatness in the land may be yours?" That is, kingship, because kings are described as possessing greatness, majesty and exaltedness. "In the land": the land of Egypt. "And we will not believe you": we will not accept as true what you have brought.

"And [yakūna] (may be)": read by Hammād and Yaḥyā.
Pharaoh said, "Bring me every learned sorcerer." Ḥamzah and ʿAlī read "saḥḥārin" (a more intensive form, "a great sorcerer").

"Ma" is a relative pronoun (*ma mawsulah*) functioning as the subject (*mubtada'*), "ji'tum bihi" is its relative clause (*sillah*), and "al-sihr" is the predicate (*khabar*). The meaning is: "That which you have brought is sorcery, not what Pharaoh and his people called sorcery, [which is] among the signs of God." "Al-sihr" is read with a pause after it by Abu 'Amr. According to this reading, "ma" is interrogative, meaning: "What is it that you have brought? Is it sorcery?"

﴿Indeed, God will nullify it﴾, that is, He will make its falsehood manifest. ﴿Indeed, God does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾, that is, He does not make it endure; rather, He destroys it. (p-36)

The meaning is: "That which you have brought is sorcery, not what Pharaoh and his people called sorcery, [which is] among the signs of God." "Al-sihr" is read with a pause after it by Abu 'Amr. ﴿Indeed, God will nullify it﴾, that is, He will make its falsehood manifest. ﴿Indeed, God does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾, that is, He does not make it endure; rather, He destroys it. (p-36)

Translation:

﴿And Allah establishes the truth﴾ and confirms it ﴿by His words﴾, that is, by His commands and decrees; or it means that Islam is made manifest by His promises of victory. ﴿Even though the criminals dislike it﴾, that is, dislike that.

﴿So none believed in Musa﴾ at the beginning of his mission, ﴿except a few of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh﴾, meaning a group of the descendants (dhurriyya, offspring) of the Children of Israel. It is as if it were said: except some children of the children of his people. This is because he called the fathers, but they did not respond to him out of fear of Pharaoh, while a group of their sons responded to him despite the fear. Or the pronoun in "his people" refers to Pharaoh, and the dhurriyya are the believer from the family of Pharaoh, Asiya his wife, his treasurer, the wife of his treasurer, and his hairdresser.

The pronoun in ﴿their chiefs﴾ refers to Pharaoh in the sense of Pharaoh's family, as one says: Rabi'a and Mudar. Or because he has companions who take counsel for him. Or it refers to the offspring, meaning: out of fear of Pharaoh and out of fear of the nobles of the Children of Israel, because they used to prevent their descendants [from believing] out of fear of Pharaoh for them and for themselves. The evidence for this is His saying ﴿that he would persecute them﴾, meaning that Pharaoh would torture them. ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh was exalted in the land﴾, meaning dominant and overpowering in it. ﴿And indeed he was among the transgressors﴾ in oppression and corruption, and in arrogance and insolence through his claim to lordship (rububiyya).

Moses said, "O my people, if you have believed in Allah" (﴿وَقالَ مُوسى يا قَوْمِ إنْ كُنْتُمْ آمَنتُمْ بِاللهِ﴾) — meaning, you have affirmed Him and His signs — "then rely upon Him" (﴿فَعَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلُوا﴾), that is, then attribute your affair to Him for protection from Pharaoh, "if you are Muslims" (﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُسْلِمِينَ﴾). Submission (al-Islam) is a condition for reliance (al-tawakkul). Submission means that they surrender their souls to Allah, that is, make them sound and sincere for Him, with no share of Satan in them, because reliance does not exist together with mixing (al-takhlit).

{"Then they said: ﴿In Allah have we put our trust.﴾ They said this only because the people were sincere. Without doubt, Allah accepted their reliance, answered their supplication, saved them, destroyed those whom they feared, and made them successors in His land. So whoever wishes to be fit for trusting in his Lord, let him abandon mixing (his intentions) and turn to sincerity (ikhlas). ﴿Our Lord, make us not a trial for the wrongdoing people.﴾ Meaning: do not make us a place of trial for them, i.e., a punishment by which they torment us, or who tempt us away from our religion, i.e., who lead us astray; and the tempter (al-fatin) is the one who misguides from the truth."}
And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people. That is: from their torment and their subjugation.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 87:

﴿And We revealed to Moses and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses into a qibla, and establish the prayer. And give good tidings to the believers."﴾

Tabawwa'a al-makan (تَبَوَّأ المَكانَ): he took it as a dwelling-place (maba'a), like his saying tawattanahu (تَوَطَّنَهُ), when he took it as a homeland (watan). The meaning is: make in Egypt houses from among its houses as a dwelling-place for your people, and a place of return to which they return for worship and prayer therein. ﴿And make your houses a qibla﴾, that is: places of prayer (masajid) facing the qibla, which is the Ka'ba. Moses and those with him used to pray towards the Ka'ba. At the beginning of the matter they were commanded to pray in their houses, in secret from the disbelievers, lest they become apparent to them, so that they would harm them and tempt them away from their religion, just as the Muslims were in that condition at the beginning of Islam in Mecca. ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ in your houses until you are safe. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, O Moses. He used the dual form in address first, then the plural, then the singular at the end, because the choice of places of worship is among what is delegated to the prophets, then the plural, because building mosques and praying in them is obligatory upon the community in general. Moses, peace be upon him, was singled out for the good tidings, honoring it and the one to whom it is given.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 10, verse 88:

﴿And Moses said: "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment﴾: this is what they adorn themselves with, of clothing, jewelry, furnishings, household goods, or other things. ﴿and wealth in the life of this world﴾, that is, cash, blessings, and estates. ﴿Our Lord, so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way.﴾ "Liyaḍillū" (لِيَضِلُّوا), that is, that they may lead the people away from Your obedience. This is the reading of the Kufans (Kūfī). There is no pause at "the world," because His saying "liyaḍillū" is linked to "ātayta" (You have given). ﴿Our Lord,﴾ the repetition of the first address is for insistence in supplication. Shaykh Abu Mansur, may Allah have mercy on him, said: When He knows that they will lead people astray from His way, He gives them what He gives them so that they will stray from His way. (p-38) This is like His saying: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178]. So the verse is a proof against the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾, that is, destroy it and remove its traces, because they use Your blessing to disobey You. "Al-ṭams" (الطَّمْس) means erasure and destruction. It was said that their dirhams and dinars turned into stones in the shape they had, with their inscriptions. It was also said that all their wealth became like that. ﴿And harden their hearts﴾, that is, seal their hearts and make them hard. ﴿So they will not believe﴾ is the answer to the supplication, which is "harden." ﴿Until they see the painful punishment﴾, that is, until they see the painful punishment. This happened, for they did not believe until they drowned, and that was the faith of despair, so it was not accepted. He only supplicated against them with this when he despaired of their faith and knew through revelation that they would not believe. But before he knew that they would not believe, it was not permissible for him to supplicate with this prayer, because he was sent to them to call them to faith. This indicates that supplicating against another that they die in disbelief is not itself disbelief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 89:

﴿He said: "Your supplication has indeed been answered."﴾ It is said: Musa (peace be upon him) was supplicating while Harun was saying "Amin," so it is established that the saying of "Amin" is a form of supplication, and therefore keeping it silent (ikhfa') is preferable. The meaning is: your supplication is answered, and what you have asked for will come to pass, but at its appointed time. ﴿So go straight﴾: remain steadfast in what you are upon of calling (to the truth) and conveying (the message). ﴿And do not follow the path of those who do not know﴾: do not follow the way of the ignorant who do not know the truthfulness of the answer and the wisdom of the delay, for between the supplication and the answer there were forty years.

"Wa-la tattabi'aanni" (with the nun lightened and kasra) was read by Ibn 'Amir (al-Shami), owing to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, likening it to the nun of the dual. Some scholars considered this an error, because the light nun (nun al-khafifah) must be sukun. It is also said that it is a report about what the two of them would be upon and not a prohibition; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal), and its implied sense is: "So go straight, not following..."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 90:

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾ — this is an proof for us regarding the creation of acts (khalq al-af'al, the doctrine that God creates human actions). ﴿Then Pharaoh and his soldiers pursued them﴾, so they caught up with them. It is said: "tabi'tuhu" (I followed him) until "atba'tuhu" (I caught up with him). ﴿Out of insolence﴾, arrogance (p-39) ﴿and enmity﴾, wrongdoing. Both words are in the accusative, either as circumstantial accusatives (hal) or as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him﴾ — there is no pause at this point, because ﴿he said: "I believe"﴾ is the answer to "idha" (when). ﴿That﴾ — "innahu" (with a kasra) is read by Hamzah and Ali as a fresh start (isti'naf), and as a substitute (badal) for "amantu." With a fatha, the others read it, by deleting the preposition ba' which is the complement of the verb of belief. ﴿There is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believed, and I am among the Muslims﴾. In this there is a proof that faith (iman) and submission (islam) are one and the same, since he said "I believe" and then said "and I am among the Muslims." Pharaoh repeated one single meaning three times in three expressions, out of eagerness for acceptance, yet it was not accepted from him, because he erred in his timing. One single instance would have sufficed in a state of free choice.

﴿Now?﴾ Do you believe at a time of compulsion, when drowning has overtaken you and you have despaired of yourself? It is said: he said this when drowning had gripped his throat, and the governing element ('āmil, the word that determines the case) in it is "Do you believe" in ﴿and you disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾, that is, among the misguided who lead others astray from faith. It is narrated that Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, came to him with a legal question (fatwa): "What is the ruling of the Amir concerning a slave of a man who was raised in his wealth and blessings, then denied his benefactor's favour, rejected his right, and claimed lordship over him?" So he wrote concerning it. Abu al-'Abbas al-Walid ibn Mus'ab says: The recompense of the slave who rebels against his master, who is a disbeliever in his favour, is that he be drowned in the sea. So when drowning gripped his throat, Jibril, peace be upon him, handed him his own handwriting, and he recognised it.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 92:**

﴿So today We shall save you﴾: We shall cast you onto a high place of the earth. The water threw him up onto the shore like a bull. ﴿with your body﴾: this is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning: in the state in which there is no spirit in you and you are only a body. Or, "with your body" means complete and sound, with nothing lacking from it and nothing changed. Or, "naked," with you being only a body without clothing. Or, "with your armor" (bi-dir‘ika), for he had a golden coat of mail by which he was known. Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) read "bi-abdānika" (with your bodies), which is like their saying "huwa bi-ajrāmihi" (he is with his bodies), meaning: with your whole body, complete in its parts, or with your armors, because he was apparent among them. ﴿So that you may be a sign for those after you﴾: a sign (ʿalāma) for those who come after you among the people, and they are the Children of Israel. In their minds was the belief that Pharaoh was too great in station to drown. It is said that Moses informed them of his destruction, but they did not believe him, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, cast him onto the shore until they saw him with their own eyes. It is also said that "those after you" refers to the generations that come after you. The meaning of his being a sign is that he shows people his servitude (ʿubūdiyya), and that what he claimed of lordship (rubūbiyya) was impossible, and that despite his great kingdom, his affair ended in what you see, due to his disobedience to his Lord, so what is to be thought of others? ﴿And indeed many of the people are heedless of Our signs.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 93:

﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a truthful abode﴾: a good and pleasing dwelling place, namely Egypt and al-Sham (Greater Syria). ﴿And We provided them with good things, and they did not differ﴾ concerning their religion ﴿until knowledge had come to them﴾, i.e., the Torah. Yet they differed concerning its interpretation, just as the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) differed concerning the interpretation of the verses of the Qur'an. Or the meaning is knowledge of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the difference of the Children of Israel, who are the People of the Book, lies in their disagreement about his description: whether he is this one or not, after knowledge had come to them that he is this one. ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾: He will distinguish the one who is in the right from the one who is in the wrong, and will recompense each one with its due recompense.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 94:

﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Book before you.﴾ When he had mentioned the Children of Israel, who are the readers of the Book, and described them as having been given knowledge, (he wished to affirm their knowledge of the soundness of the Qur'an and of the soundness of his prophethood ﷺ, because the matter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is written in the Torah and the Gospel, and they recognize him just as they recognize their own sons), and to emphasize this, he said: "If a doubt has occurred to you, supposing and assuming it" — and the way of one whom a doubt has crept into is to hasten to resolve it by returning to the principles and proofs of the religion or by discussing with the scholars — "then ask the scholars of the People of the Book, for they have such a comprehensive grasp of the soundness of what has been sent down to you that they are fit to be consulted by one like you, let alone by others." Thus the intended meaning is to describe the rabbis as firmly rooted in knowledge of the soundness of what was sent down to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, not to describe the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as doubting it. Then he said: ﴿Certainly the truth has come to you from your Lord﴾, meaning: it has been established for you, through the clear signs and manifest proofs, (p-41) that what has come to you is the truth, about which there is no room for doubt. ﴿So do not be among those who dispute﴾, meaning the doubters. The word "lest" here is not a pause, being a conjunction (ʿaṭf).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 95:**

﴿So do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ Meaning: persist and remain in what you are upon, namely the negation of doubt about you and the denial of the signs of Allah. Or it is in the manner of incitement and stirring up (al-tahyij wa al-ilhab), like His saying ﴿So never be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Qasas: 86] and ﴿And let them not avert you from the signs of Allah after they have been revealed to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 87]. It is also for the increase of firmness and protection (from error). For this reason, when it was revealed, he (peace be upon him) said: "I do not doubt, nor do I ask. Rather, I bear witness that it is the Truth." Or the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community, meaning: "And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you," like His saying ﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [al-Nisa': 174]. Or the address is to every hearer who may be subject to doubt, like the saying of the Arabs: "If your brother is honored, then congratulate him." Or *in* is a particle of negation, meaning: "So if you were not in doubt, then ask," that is, "And We do not command you to ask, because you are in doubt, but so that you may increase in certainty, just as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) increased in certainty by witnessing the giving of life to the dead."

If you say: *in* as a particle of negation only comes when it is followed by *illa* (except), as in His saying ﴿The disbelievers are only in delusion﴾ [al-Mulk: 20]. I say: that is not necessary. Do you not see His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, none could hold them after Him﴾ [Fatir: 41]? Here *in* is a particle of negation, and there is nothing after it but *illa*.

Surah 10, verse 96, from al-Nasafi's commentary (Madarik al-Tanzil):

﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified﴾ — the word of Allah that is established upon them is that which He wrote in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh) and which He informed the angels of: that they will die as disbelievers; or it is His saying, "I will surely fill Hell" (Qur'an 11:119), and so on, the verse.

There is no pause (waqf) at ﴿they will not believe﴾, because it is connected to what precedes it.

Even if every sign came to them, until they see the painful punishment. That is: at the time of despair, so they would believe, but it would not benefit them; or at the time of the Resurrection, and it would not be accepted from them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 98:

﴿Why was there not a town that believed,﴾ so that it would have been (fa-hallā: "why not"), one town among the towns We destroyed, that repented of disbelief and sincerely embraced faith before witnessing the punishment, and did not delay as Pharaoh delayed until he was seized by his death. ﴿So its faith benefited it,﴾ by God accepting its faith from it, since it occurred at a time of choice. ﴿Except the people of Yunus (Jonah),﴾ this is an exceptive clause (istithna' munqati', "disconnected exception"), meaning: "but the people of Yunus [did believe]." Or it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), and the sentence carries the sense of negation, as if it were said: no town among the destroyed towns believed except the people of Yunus. Its grammatical case (intisab) is according to the original form of the exception.

﴿When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world, and We let them enjoy (their lives) for a time,﴾ until their appointed terms.

It is narrated that Yunus, peace be upon him, was sent to Nineveh (Ninawa), from the land of Mosul, and they denied him. He departed from them in anger. When they lost him, they feared the descent of punishment, so they all wore sackcloth, cried out for forty nights, and went out to the open ground with themselves, their women, their children, and their animals, and they separated the women and children from the animals and their young, so some of them yearned for others. They displayed faith and repentance, and He had mercy on them and removed the punishment from them. That day was the Day of 'Ashura', a Friday. Their repentance reached the point that they returned the wrongs they had committed, so much so that a man would uproot a stone on which he had laid the foundation of his building and return it.

It is also said that when the punishment descended upon them, they went out to an elder from among the remnant of their scholars, and he said to them: "Say: O Living, when there is no living; O Living, who gives life to the dead; O Living, there is no god but You." So they said it, and God removed (the punishment) from them.

And from al-Fudayl, may God sanctify his spirit: they said, "O Allah, our sins have grown great and majestic, and You are greater than them and more majestic. Deal with us according to what You are worthy of, and do not deal with us according to what we deserve."

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 10, verse 99:**

﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them﴾ comprehensively and entirely, ﴿all together﴾, united in faith and in agreement upon it, not differing about it. He informed of the completeness of His power and the effectiveness of His will: that if He willed, all those on earth would have believed (p-43), but He willed that faith in Him be given to those whom He knew would choose faith in Him, and He willed disbelief for those whom He knew would choose disbelief and not believe in Him.

The Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds that human acts are created by humans) say: the intended meaning of "will" here is the will of compulsion and constraint, i.e., if He had created faith in them by force, they would have believed, but He willed that they believe by choice, so they did not believe. Their evidence is ﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾, meaning: the will to compel and coerce in matters of faith does not belong to you; that belongs to Me. This is corrupt, because faith is an act of the servant, and an act is what occurs by his power, and this cannot be realized without choice.

Our interpretation of the verse is that God Most High, by way of grace (lutf), if He had granted it to them, they would all have believed by choice; but He knew that they would not believe, so He did not grant them that, which is tawfiq (divine enabling success). The interrogative in ﴿Will you then﴾ carries the sense of negation, meaning: you do not have the power, O Muhammad, to compel them to faith, because faith is assent and affirmation, and compulsion cannot produce assent.

﴿No soul could ever believe except by the permission of Allah﴾: by His will, or by His decree, or by His enabling and facilitating, or by His knowledge. ﴿And He places the rijs (filth)﴾: that is, the punishment, or the wrath, or Satan, meaning He empowers Satan ﴿upon those who do not use reason﴾: who do not benefit from their intellects. "Wa-naj'alu" (with the nun) is the reading of Hammad and Yahya.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 101:

﴿Say: Look⦆ — a look of inference and reflection (istidlal wa i'tibar) — ﴿at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ of the signs and lessons (al-ayat wa al-ibar) in the alternation of night and day and the sprouting of crops and fruits. ﴿But of what use are signs and warnings﴾ — "ma" here is negating (nafiyah) — ﴿and warnings﴾, that is, the messengers who warn, or the warnings themselves, ﴿to a people who do not believe﴾ — whose belief is not expected, and they are those who do not use their reason (la ya'qiluna).

﴿Are they waiting for anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ That is, the events (waqa'i') of God concerning them, as it is said: "the days of the Arabs" (ayyam al-'Arab) for their battles (waqa'i'iha). ﴿Say: Then wait; I am with you among those who wait.﴾

ثُمَّ نُنَجِّي رُسُلَنا ("Then We deliver Our messengers") is coordinated with an omitted statement that is indicated by "إلّا مِثْلَ أيّامِ الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا مِن قَبْلِهِمْ" ("except like the days of those who passed away before them"). It is as if it were said: "We destroy the nations, then We deliver Our messengers," in narrating the past conditions. ﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ ("and those who believed") means whoever believed along with them. ﴿كَذَلِكَ حَقًّا عَلَيْنا نُنْجِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("Thus, it is a binding duty upon Us: We deliver the believers") means: like that deliverance, We deliver the believers from among you, and We destroy the polytheists. "وحَقًّا عَلَيْنا" ("and it is a binding duty upon Us") is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ), meaning: and that is incumbent upon Us as a binding obligation. "نُنْجِ" with the lightened pronunciation (al-takhfif) is recited by ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 104:

﴿Say, O people,﴾ that is, O people of Makkah, ﴿if you are in doubt concerning my religion﴾ and its soundness and rectitude, then this is my religion; so listen to its description. Then he described his religion, saying: ﴿then I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah﴾, that is, the idols, ﴿but I worship Allah, who causes you to die﴾, that is, who makes you die. He described Him by causing death so as to show them that He is the one truly deserving to be feared, to be guarded against, and to be worshipped, rather than that which has no power over anything. ﴿And I have been commanded to be of the believers﴾, meaning: that I should be; that is, Allah commanded me to that, by means of the intellect He placed within me and by what He revealed to me in His Book.

"And [it was revealed to me]: 'Set your face upright toward the religion'" — that is, "and it was revealed to me, 'that set [your face]'," in order to match His words "I have been commanded" (ukirtu), meaning: be upright, turning your face toward what Allah has commanded you, or be upright toward it, and do not turn right or left. ﴿Hanīfan﴾ (upright, in pure monotheistic devotion) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) modifying either "the religion" or "the face." ﴿And do not be among the polytheists.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 106:

﴿And do not call upon, other than Allah, that which can neither benefit you﴾ if you call upon it, ﴿nor harm you﴾ if you forsake it. ﴿But if you do it﴾, meaning if you call upon other than Allah that which neither benefits nor harms you, ﴿then you would be among the wrongdoers﴾. Here the act is referred to by the verb alone, for the sake of brevity. ﴿Then you would be among the wrongdoers﴾: "idhan" (then, in that case) is the response to the condition and an answer to an implied question, as if a questioner had asked about the consequence of worshipping idols, and it was said that one would be among the wrongdoers, because there is no wrongdoing greater than shirk (associating partners with Allah).

﴿And if God touches you﴾ with ﴿harm﴾, meaning sickness, ﴿there is none who can remove it﴾, that harm, ﴿except Him﴾, except God. ﴿And if He intends for you good﴾, meaning health, ﴿there is none who can repel His bounty﴾, meaning none who can repel His will. ﴿He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants with it﴾, with the good. By this verse He cut off from His servants the path of desire and dread except toward Him, and of reliance except upon Him. ﴿And He is the Forgiving﴾, who expiates through affliction, ﴿the Merciful﴾, who grants well-being through giving.

He follows the prohibition of worshipping idols, and describing them as neither benefiting nor harming, with the statement that God is the one who harms and benefits. If He afflicts you with harm, none can remove it except Him alone, to the exclusion of everyone. How, then, [could it be] with an inanimate object that has no awareness? Likewise, if He intends good for you, no one can repel what He wills for you of bounty and kindness. How then with idols? He is worthy, therefore, that worship be directed to Him rather than to them. This is more eloquent than His saying: ﴿If God intends harm for me, can they remove His harm? Or if He intends mercy for me, can they withhold His mercy?﴾ [al-Zumar: 38]. He mentioned "touch" in one and "intention" in the other, as if He wished to mention both matters: the intending and the afflicting, in each of the two kinds of harm, and that none can repel what He intends of them or remove what He afflicts with them. So He was concise, mentioning "touch," which is affliction, in one, and "intention" in the other, so that what was mentioned would indicate what was omitted. Moreover, He mentioned affliction with good in His saying: ﴿He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants with it﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 108:

﴿Say: O mankind,﴾ O people of Makkah, ﴿the truth has come to you from your Lord.﴾ The truth is the Qur'an or the Messenger. ﴿So whoever is guided﴾ chooses guidance and follows the truth, ﴿then he is guided only for his own self.﴾ So by his choice he benefits none but himself. ﴿And whoever goes astray, then he strays only to its detriment.﴾ Whoever prefers misguidance, then he harms none but himself. The lam (la, "for") and ʿalā (ʿala, "against") indicate the meaning of benefit and harm. ﴿And I am not over you a guardian.﴾ A guardian (wakil) is one entrusted with your affairs, a keeper to whom your matter is committed. ﴿I am only a bringer of good news and a warner.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 10, verse 109:

﴿And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient﴾ over their denial and their harm to you, ﴿until Allah judges﴾ in your favour over them, granting you victory and dominance, ﴿and He is the best of judges﴾, because He is the One who knows the hidden secrets, so He has no need of proof or witnesses.
